<div class="thumbinner mp-thumb" style="background: transparent; color: inherit; border: none; padding: 0; max-width: 172px;">
<span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:French_battleship_Brennus_NH_64443.jpg" class="mw-file-description" title="French battleship Brennus"><img alt="French battleship Brennus" src="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/96/French_battleship_Brennus_NH_64443.jpg/250px-French_battleship_Brennus_NH_64443.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail" decoding="async" loading="lazy" width="172" height="115" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/96/French_battleship_Brennus_NH_64443.jpg/500px-French_battleship_Brennus_NH_64443.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail 2x" data-file-width="5744" data-file-height="3824"/></a></span></div></div>
<p><i><b><a href="/wiki/French_battleship_Brennus" title="French battleship Brennus">Brennus</a></b></i> was the first <a href="/wiki/Pre-dreadnought_battleship" title="Pre-dreadnought battleship">pre-dreadnought battleship</a> built for the <a href="/wiki/French_Navy" title="French Navy">French Navy</a>. Launched on 17 October 1891, she was an <a href="/wiki/Ironclad_warship" title="Ironclad warship">ironclad battleship</a> with a <a href="/wiki/Main_battery" title="Main battery">main battery</a> of heavy guns mounted on the centerline and the first use of Belleville boilers. She formed the basis for subsequent designs, beginning with <i><a href="/wiki/French_battleship_Charles_Martel" title="French battleship Charles Martel">Charles Martel</a></i>. When completed in 1893, <i>Brennus</i> was very top-heavy and had to be rebuilt over the next three years before she was ready to enter service. She spent the majority of her service in the <a href="/wiki/Commander-in-Chief,_Mediterranean_(France)" title="Commander-in-Chief, Mediterranean (France)">Mediterranean Squadron</a> and she served as its <a href="/wiki/Flagship" title="Flagship">flagship</a> early in her career. As newer battleships were commissioned into the fleet, <i>Brennus</i> was relegated to the <a href="/wiki/Reserve_fleet" title="Reserve fleet">Reserve Squadron</a> in the early 1900s and then served as a <a href="/wiki/Training_ship" title="Training ship">training ship</a>. The ship was decommissioned before the First World War began in August 1914 and disarmed in 1915. She served as a source of spare parts and equipment for other ships during the war. Her <a href="/wiki/Hulk_(ship_type)" title="Hulk (ship type)">hulk</a> was stricken from the <a href="/wiki/Navy_Directory" title="Navy Directory">naval register</a> in 1919 and was <a href="/wiki/Ship_breaking" title="Ship breaking">scrapped</a> three years later. <i>(<b><a href="/wiki/French_battleship_Brennus" title="French battleship Brennus">Full article...</a></b>)</i>
</p>

<div class="thumbinner mp-thumb" style="background: transparent; color: inherit; border: none; padding: 0; max-width: 126px;">
<span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Avery_Hopwood.png" class="mw-file-description" title="Avery Hopwood"><img alt="Avery Hopwood" src="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/Avery_Hopwood.png/250px-Avery_Hopwood.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail" decoding="async" loading="lazy" width="126" height="155" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/Avery_Hopwood.png/330px-Avery_Hopwood.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail 2x" data-file-width="603" data-file-height="742"/></a></span><div class="thumbcaption" style="padding: 0.25em 0; word-wrap: break-word;">Avery Hopwood</div></div></div>
<p><i><b><a href="/wiki/The_Demi-Virgin" title="The Demi-Virgin">The Demi-Virgin</a></b></i> is a play written by <a href="/wiki/Avery_Hopwood" title="Avery Hopwood">Avery Hopwood</a> <i>(pictured)</i>. Producer <a href="/wiki/A._H._Woods" title="A. H. Woods">A. H. Woods</a> staged it on <a href="/wiki/Broadway_theatre" title="Broadway theatre">Broadway</a>; it premiered on October 18, 1921, and was one of the most successful plays of the season. The play is a <a href="/wiki/Bedroom_farce" title="Bedroom farce">bedroom farce</a> about former couple Gloria Graham and Wally Deane, both movie actors, whose marriage was so brief that the press speculated about Gloria's virginity. Because it contained suggestive dialog and the female cast wore revealing clothes, the production was considered highly risqué at the time. The script alluded to a contemporary scandal involving actor <a href="/wiki/Roscoe_Arbuckle" title="Roscoe Arbuckle">Roscoe Arbuckle</a>. Reviewers panned the play as unfunny and vulgar. A magistrate ruled the play was obscene, and <a href="/wiki/United_States_obscenity_law" title="United States obscenity law">obscenity</a> charges were brought against Woods, but a <a href="/wiki/Grand_jury" title="Grand jury">grand jury</a> declined to <a href="/wiki/Indictment" title="Indictment">indict</a> him. Woods promoted the controversy to increase ticket sales. The play had no long-term literary impact and was never published, but it stimulated arguments over <a href="/wiki/Censorship" title="Censorship">censorship</a> of theatrical performances. <i>(<b><a href="/wiki/The_Demi-Virgin" title="The Demi-Virgin">Full article...</a></b>)</i>
</p>

<span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Achaemenid_Cappadocia.jpg" class="mw-file-description" title="The Satrapy of Cappadocia (dark red) c. 500 BC"><img alt="The Satrapy of Cappadocia (dark red) c. 500 BC" src="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4b/Achaemenid_Cappadocia.jpg/250px-Achaemenid_Cappadocia.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail" decoding="async" loading="lazy" width="168" height="117" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4b/Achaemenid_Cappadocia.jpg/500px-Achaemenid_Cappadocia.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail 2x" data-file-width="996" data-file-height="694"/></a></span><div class="thumbcaption" style="padding: 0.25em 0; word-wrap: break-word;">The Satrapy of Cappadocia (dark red) <abbr title="circa">c.</abbr><span style="white-space:nowrap;"> 500 BC</span></div></div></div>
<p>The <b><a href="/wiki/Ancient_Cappadocian_language" title="Ancient Cappadocian language">ancient Cappadocian language</a></b> is an <a href="/wiki/Attested_language" title="Attested language">unattested language</a> once spoken in <a href="/wiki/Classical_antiquity" title="Classical antiquity">antiquity</a> in <a href="/wiki/Cappadocia" title="Cappadocia">Cappadocia</a>, a historical region of central <a href="/wiki/Anatolia" title="Anatolia">Anatolia</a> in modern-day <a href="/wiki/Turkey" title="Turkey">Turkey</a> <i>(map pictured)</i>. There are no known texts written in Cappadocian, although classical Greek writers identified Cappadocian as distinct from Greek, and a few Greek words were attributed to a Cappadocian origin. The language also influenced the pronunciation of Greek spoken by Cappadocians, whose accent was infamous among classical authors. Although Cappadocian does not have a secure linguistic classification, it likely belonged to the <a href="/wiki/Anatolian_languages" title="Anatolian languages">Anatolian branch</a> of the <a href="/wiki/Indo-European_languages" title="Indo-European languages">Indo-European languages</a>, probably as a relative or descendant of <a href="/wiki/Luwian_language" title="Luwian language">Luwian</a>. Prior to the modern understanding of Anatolian languages in the twentieth century, Cappadocian was variously considered part of the <a href="/wiki/Semitic_languages" title="Semitic languages">Semitic</a> family, part of other known branches of Indo-European, or part of an Anatolian language family unrelated to any other known languages. <i>(<b><a href="/wiki/Ancient_Cappadocian_language" title="Ancient Cappadocian language">Full article...</a></b>)</i>
</p>

		<summary type="html"><div class="mw-content-ltr mw-parser-output" lang="en" dir="ltr"><div id="mp-tfa-img" style="float: left; margin: 0.5em 0.9em 0.4em 0em;">
<div class="thumbinner mp-thumb" style="background: transparent; color: inherit; border: none; padding: 0; max-width: 115px;">
<span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:The_monster_cutting_a_lady.jpg" class="mw-file-description" title="Cartoon of the London Monster"><img alt="Cartoon of the London Monster" src="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/The_monster_cutting_a_lady.jpg/120px-The_monster_cutting_a_lady.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail" decoding="async" loading="lazy" width="115" height="170" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/The_monster_cutting_a_lady.jpg/250px-The_monster_cutting_a_lady.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail 2x" data-file-width="1101" data-file-height="1631"/></a></span><div class="thumbcaption" style="padding: 0.25em 0; word-wrap: break-word;">Cartoon of the London Monster</div></div></div>
<p>The <b><a href="/wiki/London_Monster" title="London Monster">London Monster</a></b> was the name given to an attacker of women in London between 1788 and 1790. The Monster's <i><a href="/wiki/Modus_operandi" title="Modus operandi">modus operandi</a></i> was to abuse women verbally with lewd and suggestive comments, then attack them with a knife <i>(cartoon pictured)</i>. The philanthropist <a href="/wiki/John_Julius_Angerstein" title="John Julius Angerstein">John Julius Angerstein</a> arranged a reward of 100 guineas (equivalent to £13,000 in 2025) for the capture and conviction of the Monster. More than 30 men were taken to <a href="/wiki/Bow_Street_Magistrates%27_Court_and_Police_Station" title="Bow Street Magistrates' Court and Police Station">Bow Street Magistrates' Court</a> with their accusers hoping to claim the reward; all were released. Renwick Williams was arrested when one of the attacked women claimed to recognise him as the attacker. He was found guilty, despite having an <a href="/wiki/Alibi" title="Alibi">alibi</a> for at least one of the attacks. There is doubt among some historians whether he was the attacker as no hard or forensic evidence was ever found. It is likely that <a href="/wiki/Copycat_crime" title="Copycat crime">copycat attacks</a> took place, particularly as some of the assaults were recorded as being committed by a group of men. <i>(<b><a href="/wiki/London_Monster" title="London Monster">Full article...</a></b>)</i>
</p>

<p>The <b><a href="/wiki/Hongwu_Emperor" title="Hongwu Emperor">Hongwu Emperor</a></b> (21 October 1328 – 24 June 1398), personal name Zhu Yuanzhang, was the founding <a href="/wiki/List_of_emperors_of_the_Ming_dynasty" title="List of emperors of the Ming dynasty">emperor of the Ming dynasty</a> of China, reigning from 1368 to 1398. Born into a peasant family in <a href="/wiki/Anhui" title="Anhui">Anhui</a>, Zhu grew up amid famine, epidemics, and unrest under the Mongol-led <a href="/wiki/Yuan_dynasty" title="Yuan dynasty">Yuan dynasty</a>. Orphaned at 16, he briefly lived as a novice monk before joining the <a href="/wiki/Red_Turban_Rebellions" title="Red Turban Rebellions">Red Turban rebels</a> in 1352. Rising rapidly, he captured <a href="/wiki/Nanjing" title="Nanjing">Nanjing</a> in 1356, established a regional regime, and defeated rival rebels. In 1368, he proclaimed the <a href="/wiki/Ming_dynasty" title="Ming dynasty">Ming dynasty</a>, adopted the <a href="/wiki/Chinese_era_name" title="Chinese era name">era name</a> <a href="/wiki/Hongwu_era" title="Hongwu era">Hongwu</a>, and expelled the Yuan from <a href="/wiki/China_proper" title="China proper">China proper</a>. During his 30-year reign, he restored stability after decades of war, strengthened state institutions, promoted agriculture, and maintained a disciplined army while seeking to limit civilian suffering. He died in 1398 and was succeeded by his grandson, the <a href="/wiki/Jianwen_Emperor" title="Jianwen Emperor">Jianwen Emperor</a>, who was <a href="/wiki/Jingnan_campaign" title="Jingnan campaign">overthrown in 1402</a> by <a href="/wiki/Yongle_Emperor" title="Yongle Emperor">Zhu Di</a>, later known as the Yongle Emperor. <i>(<b><a href="/wiki/Hongwu_Emperor" title="Hongwu Emperor">Full article...</a></b>)</i>
</p>

<span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Priestfield1.jpg" class="mw-file-description" title="Priestfield Stadium, Gillingham's home ground"><img alt="Priestfield Stadium, Gillingham's home ground" src="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Priestfield1.jpg/250px-Priestfield1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail" decoding="async" loading="lazy" width="170" height="116" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Priestfield1.jpg/500px-Priestfield1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail 2x" data-file-width="691" data-file-height="470"/></a></span><div class="thumbcaption" style="padding: 0.25em 0; word-wrap: break-word;">Priestfield Stadium, Gillingham's home ground</div></div></div>
<p>In <b><a href="/wiki/1986%E2%80%9387_Gillingham_F.C._season" title="1986–87 Gillingham F.C. season">their <span class="nowrap">1986–87</span> season</a></b>, <a href="/wiki/Gillingham_F.C." title="Gillingham F.C.">Gillingham F.C.</a> competed in the <a href="/wiki/Football_League_Third_Division" title="Football League Third Division">Football League Third Division</a>. Gillingham were at the top of the Third Division table shortly before the mid-point of the season; their form declined in the second half of the season and they finished in fifth place, qualifying for the play-offs. Gillingham faced <a href="/wiki/Swindon_Town_F.C." title="Swindon Town F.C.">Swindon Town</a> in the <a href="/wiki/1987_Football_League_Third_Division_play-off_final" title="1987 Football League Third Division play-off final">1987 Third Division final</a> where, after drawing <span class="nowrap">2–2</span> on aggregate, they lost <span class="nowrap">2–0</span> in the <a href="/wiki/Replay_(sports)" title="Replay (sports)">replay</a>. Gillingham reached the third round of the <a href="/wiki/FA_Cup" title="FA Cup">FA Cup</a>, the second round of the <a href="/wiki/EFL_Cup" title="EFL Cup">Football League Cup</a>, and the southern section semi-finals of the <a href="/wiki/EFL_Trophy" title="EFL Trophy">Associate Members' Cup</a>. Gillingham played 63 competitive matches, winning 31, drawing 12 and losing 20. <a href="/wiki/Tony_Cascarino" title="Tony Cascarino">Tony Cascarino</a> was the club's leading goalscorer, with 30 goals in all competitions. <a href="/wiki/Howard_Pritchard" title="Howard Pritchard">Howard Pritchard</a> and <a href="/wiki/Paul_Haylock" title="Paul Haylock">Paul Haylock</a> made the most appearances; both played in 62 matches. The highest attendance recorded at the club's home ground, <a href="/wiki/Priestfield_Stadium" title="Priestfield Stadium">Priestfield Stadium</a> <i>(pictured)</i>, was 16,775, for the home leg of the play-off final. <i>(<b><a href="/wiki/1986%E2%80%9387_Gillingham_F.C._season" title="1986–87 Gillingham F.C. season">Full article...</a></b>)</i>
</p>

<span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Thugs_About_To_Strangle_Traveller.jpg" class="mw-file-description" title="Thugs about to strangle a traveller"><img alt="Thugs about to strangle a traveller" src="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8d/Thugs_About_To_Strangle_Traveller.jpg/250px-Thugs_About_To_Strangle_Traveller.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail" decoding="async" loading="lazy" width="156" height="126" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8d/Thugs_About_To_Strangle_Traveller.jpg/330px-Thugs_About_To_Strangle_Traveller.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail 2x" data-file-width="1024" data-file-height="826"/></a></span><div class="thumbcaption" style="padding: 0.25em 0; word-wrap: break-word;">Thugs about to strangle a traveller</div></div></div>
<p><b><a href="/wiki/Thuggee" title="Thuggee">Thuggee</a></b> was a phenomenon of <a href="/wiki/Highwayman" title="Highwayman">highway robbery</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Indian_subcontinent" title="Indian subcontinent">Indian subcontinent</a> that saw <a href="/wiki/Gang" title="Gang">gangs</a> of Thugs murder and rob travellers, often by <a href="/wiki/Strangling" title="Strangling">strangling</a>. During the British colonial era, thuggee came to be represented and popularised as a secret pan-Indian <a href="/wiki/Fraternity" title="Fraternity">fraternity</a> of <a href="/wiki/Human_sacrifice" title="Human sacrifice">ritual stranglers</a> with ancient origins, motivated by <a href="/wiki/Religious_fanaticism" title="Religious fanaticism">fanaticism</a> and bloodlust. In the 1830s, colonial administrator <a href="/wiki/William_Henry_Sleeman" title="William Henry Sleeman">William Henry Sleeman</a> led a policing campaign against thuggee, supported by <a href="/wiki/Thuggee_and_Dacoity_Suppression_Acts,_1836%E2%80%9348" title="Thuggee and Dacoity Suppression Acts, 1836–48">legal developments</a> that facilitated convictions. The success of the 1839 novel <i><a href="/wiki/Confessions_of_a_Thug_(novel)" title="Confessions of a Thug (novel)">Confessions of a Thug</a></i> inspired a number of depictions in literature and film, among them <i><a href="/wiki/Indiana_Jones_and_the_Temple_of_Doom" title="Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom">Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom</a></i> (1984). Historians have since <a href="/wiki/Historical_revisionism" title="Historical revisionism">revised</a> the 19th-century portrayal, generally viewing the Thugs as more or less ordinary criminals, or thuggee as a type of <a href="/wiki/Banditry" title="Banditry">banditry</a>. There is a general consensus among contemporary historians against the colonial-era representation. <i>(<b><a href="/wiki/Thuggee" title="Thuggee">Full article...</a></b>)</i>

<span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:BW41_Schliengen.jpg" class="mw-file-description" title="Present-day view of the Schliengen battlefield"><img alt="Present-day view of the Schliengen battlefield" src="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1d/BW41_Schliengen.jpg/250px-BW41_Schliengen.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail" decoding="async" loading="lazy" width="166" height="118" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1d/BW41_Schliengen.jpg/500px-BW41_Schliengen.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail 2x" data-file-width="2872" data-file-height="2042"/></a></span><div class="thumbcaption" style="padding: 0.25em 0; word-wrap: break-word;">Present-day view of the Schliengen battlefield</div></div></div>
<p>The <b><a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Schliengen" title="Battle of Schliengen">Battle of Schliengen</a></b> took place on 24 October 1796 between the French <a href="/wiki/Army_of_the_Rhine_and_Moselle" title="Army of the Rhine and Moselle">Army of the Rhine and Moselle</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Austrian_Army_during_the_French_Revolutionary_and_Napoleonic_Wars" title="Austrian Army during the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars">Austrian army</a> near the village of <a href="/wiki/Schliengen" title="Schliengen">Schliengen</a> during the <a href="/wiki/War_of_the_First_Coalition" title="War of the First Coalition">War of the First Coalition</a>. Control of the area gave either combatant access to southwestern German states and <a href="/wiki/Rhine" title="Rhine">Rhine</a> crossings. On 20 October, the French army under <a href="/wiki/Jean_Victor_Marie_Moreau" title="Jean Victor Marie Moreau">Jean-Victor Moreau</a> retreated from <a href="/wiki/Freiburg_im_Breisgau" title="Freiburg im Breisgau">Freiburg im Breisgau</a> and established his army along a ridge of hills. The Austrian army led by <a href="/wiki/Archduke_Charles,_Duke_of_Teschen" title="Archduke Charles, Duke of Teschen">Archduke Charles</a> attacked the French flanks directly, and in force, which increased casualties for both sides. The French withdrew from the battlefield in good order and several days later crossed the Rhine at <a href="/wiki/Huningue" title="Huningue">Huningue</a>. Confusion in <a href="/wiki/Vienna" title="Vienna">Vienna</a> wasted any strategic advantage that Charles might have obtained and locked the <a href="/wiki/House_of_Habsburg" title="House of Habsburg">Habsburg</a> force into two sieges on the Rhine, when the troops were badly needed in northern Italy. The battle is commemorated on a monument in Vienna and on the <a href="/wiki/Arc_de_Triomphe" title="Arc de Triomphe">Arc de Triomphe</a> in Paris. <i>(<b><a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Schliengen" title="Battle of Schliengen">Full article...</a></b>)</i>
</p>

<p><b><a href="/wiki/The_Kinks" title="The Kinks">The Kinks</a></b> were an English rock band formed in London in 1962. Their original line-up comprised brothers <a href="/wiki/Ray_Davies" title="Ray Davies">Ray Davies</a> and <a href="/wiki/Dave_Davies" title="Dave Davies">Dave Davies</a>, <a href="/wiki/Pete_Quaife" title="Pete Quaife">Pete Quaife</a> and <a href="/wiki/Mick_Avory" title="Mick Avory">Mick Avory</a>. Emerging during the height of <a href="/wiki/British_rhythm_and_blues" title="British rhythm and blues">British rhythm and blues</a> and <a href="/wiki/Beat_music" title="Beat music">Merseybeat</a>, "<a href="/wiki/You_Really_Got_Me" title="You Really Got Me">You Really Got Me</a>" (1964), their breakthrough third single written by Ray Davies, became an international hit, topping the charts in the United Kingdom and reaching the top 10 in the United States. They were part of the <a href="/wiki/British_Invasion" title="British Invasion">British Invasion</a> until <a href="/wiki/The_Kinks%27_1965_US_tour" title="The Kinks' 1965 US tour">their 1965 American tour</a> led to them being banned from touring there for a number of years. The Kinks are regarded as one of the most influential rock bands of the 1960s. They had seventeen top-20 singles and five top-10 albums in the UK, and five singles reached the top 10 on the US <a href="/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100" title="Billboard Hot 100"><i>Billboard</i> Hot 100</a>. The band has sold more than 50 million records worldwide. In 1990, the original four members of the Kinks were inducted into the <a href="/wiki/Rock_and_Roll_Hall_of_Fame" title="Rock and Roll Hall of Fame">Rock and Roll Hall of Fame</a>, as well as the <a href="/wiki/UK_Music_Hall_of_Fame" title="UK Music Hall of Fame">UK Music Hall of Fame</a> in 2005. <i>(<b><a href="/wiki/The_Kinks" title="The Kinks">Full article...</a></b>)</i>
</p>

<p><i><b><a href="/wiki/Eyebrow_Talk" title="Eyebrow Talk">Eyebrow Talk</a></b></i> was a Chinese monthly <a href="/wiki/Literary_magazine" title="Literary magazine">literary magazine</a> published in 18 issues from 1914 to 1916. Among the first Chinese literary magazines marketed towards women, and the first to be edited mainly by women, it was founded by Gao Jianhua and Xu Xiaotian, her husband and cousin. The magazine often ran <a href="/wiki/Romance_novel" title="Romance novel">romance stories</a> aimed at women, but contained sexually explicit depictions of women in its advertising, covers, and pictures, some sourced from <a href="/wiki/French_postcard" title="French postcard">European erotic postcards</a>. Unlike its contemporaries, <i>Eyebrow Talk</i><span class="nowrap" style="padding-left:0.1em;">'s</span> romances often centered on the desires of their female protagonists, frequently including <a href="/wiki/Love_triangle" title="Love triangle">love triangles</a> between the protagonists and multiple men. Its <a href="/wiki/Libertine" title="Libertine">libertine</a> content ran afoul of a government advisory committee, who unanimously voted to ban it in 1916, making it the first Chinese magazine to be banned under charges of <a href="/wiki/Obscenity" title="Obscenity">obscenity</a>. Its association with lowbrow "<a href="/wiki/Mandarin_Ducks_and_Butterflies" title="Mandarin Ducks and Butterflies">Mandarin Duck and Butterfly</a>" fiction prevented scholarly research for much of the 20th century. <i>(<b><a href="/wiki/Eyebrow_Talk" title="Eyebrow Talk">Full article...</a></b>)</i>
